title: Das Kapital: Kritik der politischen Ökonomie
author: Karl Marx
publication_date: Volume I: 1867; Volume II: 1885; Volume III: 1894
edition_analyzed: Penguin Classics English translation, Volume I (most referenced standard edition for English readers)
target_audience: Advanced students of politics, philosophy, and history
Readers interested in the critique of capitalism and historical materialism
core_themes: Critique of capitalist production and its social consequences
Exploitation of labor and surplus value
primary_purpose: To provide a rigorous, scientific critique of the capitalist mode of production, expose its exploitative dynamics, and lay the theoretical foundation for revolutionary transformation of society.

structure_format.narrative_style: Dense, analytical, and systematic; employs dialectical reasoning and historical analysis
structure_format.organization: Divided into volumes and sections: Commodity and Money, The Transformation of Money into Capital, The Production of Absolute and Relative Surplus-Value, The Accumulation of Capital, and historical tendencies of capitalist accumulation
features: Extensive use of deductive logic and empirical evidence
Frequent references to historical events and economic data
In-depth footnotes and critiques of contemporary economists

key_concepts_lessons: Commodities have use-value and exchange-value; labor is the source of value under capitalism.
Surplus value is created through the exploitation of workers, who produce more value than they receive in wages.
Capital is not just money, but a social relation of production involving continual accumulation and reinvestment.
Commodity fetishism obscures the social relations behind production and exchange.
Capitalism is marked by cycles of boom and bust, resulting in crises that stem from its internal contradictions.
Historical progression is driven by class struggle, with capitalism containing the seeds of its own transformation.
notable_features: Foundational text for Marxist economic and social theory
Deep critique of both classical and contemporary political economy
Introduction of concepts that became central to socialist and communist movements
Influential across economics, sociology, history, and political science
Contains detailed analyses of real historical developments and case studies
cultural_historical_context: Written during the height of the Industrial Revolution, amid massive social upheaval and the rise of modern capitalism in Europe. Marx drew on the works of earlier economists and observed the conditions of workers in 19th-century factories. The publication of Das Kapital marked a pivotal moment in radical politics and socioeconomic critique, inspiring socialist movements and labor unions.
reception_impact: Regarded as one of the most influential works in social science and political theory
Foundation of Marxist economics and a key influence on socialist and communist thought worldwide
Praised for its in-depth analysis but often criticized for its complexity and occasionally dense prose
Heavily debated and interpreted in a variety of ways by subsequent generations of scholars, activists, and critics
Continues to inform analyses of capitalism and inspire activism
comparable_titles: The Wealth of Nations by Adam Smith
Principles of Political Economy and Taxation by David Ricardo
Capitalism and Freedom by Milton Friedman
The Communist Manifesto by Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels
Imperialism: The Highest Stage of Capitalism by Vladimir Lenin
